run.experiment: throughput under 20-way concurrency, TypeScript SDK: 2000 independent sleeping tasks per rep
run.host: AWS EC2 m7i.8xlarge, 32 vCPU, 123 GiB, us-east-2, Ubuntu 24.04.5, Docker 29.1.3, compose 2.40.3
run.exclusivity: Hatchet, its Postgres, the single worker and the trigger client were the only things on the box

hatchet.config: stock hatchet-lite compose, unmodified, except Postgres started with max_connections=500 (the same compose file as the earlier Python run on this study; it is not a Hatchet tuning knob)

typescript.measured_in: docker exec bench-fleet-ts node dist/versions.js, i.e. the same container the task bodies ran in

slots.verified: GET /api/v1/tenants/{tenant}/worker reported slotConfig.default = {limit: 20, available: 20} and runtimeInfo {language: TYPESCRIPT, languageVersion: v22.23.3, sdkVersion: 1.36.0}
slots.why: every engine in this study runs at the same 20-way concurrency; Hatchet's own default would have been 100

workload.cpu_not_measured: a naive recursive fibo runs about ten times faster in Node than in CPython, so a CPU-bound body would compare V8 against CPython instead of Hatchet against itself. The 100ms sleep costs the same wall-clock time in both languages, which is what makes the two runs comparable.

procedure.pre_enqueue: the worker is paused through PATCH /api/v1/workers/{id} {isPaused:true}, 0.5s is allowed for the assignment loop to observe it, the 2000 runs are bulk-triggered with runManyNoWait, then the worker is unpaused
procedure.bulk_trigger: the TypeScript SDK splits runManyNoWait into chunks of 500 (its default batchSize) and sends them serially over BulkTriggerWorkflow gRPC; the whole enqueue took 0.23-0.25s inside a 0.74-0.75s paused window
procedure.timing_source: Hatchet's own Postgres: created_at from v1_tasks_olap.inserted_at, started_at/completed_at from the STARTED and FINISHED rows in v1_task_events_olap. Harness wall-clock is recorded but never used for throughput.
